Suivre sa famille au bout du monde: Following Family to the Ends of the Earth
M. Wei, qui préfère taire son prénom, pr: Mr. Wei, who prefers not to share his first name, is taking life easy

Mr. Wei, who prefers not to share his first name, is taking life easy. Living in Montréal for more than 10 years, the Shanghai native spends his days quietly, alone in his apartment when he isn’t feeding his passion for travel. The 74-year-old hasn’t always had an easy life. From his arduous migration journey, which led him to the Montréal community, to the tragedy that brought him closer to his only daughter, he tells us his story.
<strong>‍</strong>« Ma fille souhaitait: ‍“My daughter wanted to immigrate. She took me on a visit to Canada to see if I would like it. I liked it a lot,” he says. So began his long journey, which took him from Shanghai to Montréal. Mei*, Mr. Wei’s daughter, married a Quebecer and left her father to settle in Montréal in the mid-2000s. As is the tradition in Shanghainese families, father and daughter wanted to live near each other so they could support one another. However, it would take them four and a half years to be reunited. They had to wait for Mr. Wei’s immigration file to be approved by the Canadian government. During those long years of waiting, with an ocean separating him from his family, Mr. Wei felt very alone.
« J’étais si heureux d’arriver à Montréa: “I was so happy to arrive in Montréal! I could finally be with my daughter. We would be able to take care of each other,” he exclaims. The distance between Montréal and Shanghai had made mutual support difficult. “Seniors like me always hope the next generation will be able to take care of us,” explains the man in his seventies. When asked how he experiences the contrast between his hometown and his adopted city, Mr. Wei doesn’t dwell on the cultural differences between the two metropolises. He talks about Mei. “The difference between the two is that my daughter is here! In China, I was alone,” he cries out. This close bond developed against a backdrop of tragedy.
La femme de M. Wei est décédée alors que: Mr. Wei’s wife died when their only daughter was just five years old. The loss was a heavy blow for the young working-class family. “My daughter lost her mother very young. My mother, meaning her paternal grandmother, and I raised her,” he recalls. “Working and raising a child to adulthood without my wife was very hard.”
M. Wei et sa mère y sont parvenus en sou: Mr. Wei and his mother managed by supporting the family with their respective jobs as an electrician and a seamstress. As a result, the Wei family is very close-knit. Mr. Wei, who has always had a good relationship with his daughter, has always supported her in her plans, including her decision to immigrate to Canada.
‍<strong>Les défis quotidiens de la vie: ‍The daily challenges of life in Montréal
<strong>‍</strong>Les 10 années passées: ‍The 10 years spent in Montréal haven’t been a walk in the park. The cold season is still a challenge. “I can’t stand winter! I stay home, I avoid going out because of the cold,” he lets slip. Mei helps him stay warm. “She had all my groceries delivered during the winter,” he says. And it’s not just the temperature that worries Mr. Wei. A few years ago, he fractured his hand when he fell during a winter outing. He has no desire to repeat the experience.
D’autres obstacles, comme la barrière de: Other obstacles, such as the language barrier and unfamiliarity with Quebec culture, also get in the way of his daily life. Mr. Wei therefore greatly appreciates the support he receives from the Service à la famille chinoise du Grand Montréal. “I’ve known one of the organization’s social workers for several years. She has helped me solve problems and find my way through Quebec institutions,” he says. He also gets support from his daughter’s Shanghainese friends in Quebec, who help him in situations where he has to speak French or English.
<strong>‍</strong>Il y a cinq ans, sa vi: ‍Five years ago, his social life took a positive turn when he discovered a group of Shanghainese people in Montréal. “We all come from the same region, so we have a lot in common. We get together to chat, eat, enjoy Montréal’s nightlife and travel,” he says. Travelling is his favourite of those activities. “I like it when we all pile into a big tour bus and spend the ride having fun, talking and laughing,” Mr. Wei exclaims. It’s this passion for travel that prompts him, every summer, to join a Chinese travel agency that takes him to explore North America. And although he has visited Mexico, the United States and several parts of Canada, his favourite destination remains Niagara.
« Ces chutes sont spectaculaires ! Il n’: “The falls are spectacular! There’s nothing like them anywhere else in the world,” he exclaims. “I’ve already been twice and, when I get the chance, I want to go back. I dream of taking a ride on the Maid of the Mist boat and seeing the falls from below.”
On espère qu’il pourra réaliser son rêve: We hope he will be able to realize his dream and get back to travelling soon.
